conversation_lines.text: The tingling could be from vitamin deficiencies. We’re giving you thiamine, folic acid, and multivitamins. That should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been eating much. Just not hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. Your labs show low potassium, magnesium, and phosphate. That’s from malnutrition and alcohol use. We’re replacing those carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I feel so weak?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Also, your body is recovering. We’re giving you Ensure supplements to help with nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lactate was high yesterday—3.6—but it’s coming down. That’s a good sign your body is recovering from stress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does lactate mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a marker of how well your body is using oxygen. High levels can mean stress or poor perfusion. Yours is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My legs are more swollen now, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noticed. You have diastolic heart failure. Your heart doesn’t relax well, so fluid builds up. You weren’t taking your water pills regularly, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Only when my legs got really puffy. I didn’t like peeing so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on furosemide and spironolactone to help. You’ll need to take them daily, even if you feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I have to take them forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely yes, to protect your heart and prevent fluid overload. We’ll adjust the dose based on how you feel and your labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium is low—3.3. We’re adding a potassium supplement to your meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the water pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Also from poor intake and your liver disease. We’re giving you 20 mEq daily to keep it safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about my anemia? My blood count was low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have iron deficiency. Ferritin was 50—low normal. We’re starting ferrous sulfate. You’ll need a colonoscopy later to check for sources.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t have bleeding or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes it’s silent. Given your history, we want to rule out anything serious in the gut.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your edema is improving. The diuretics are working. We’ll keep you on them after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I can breathe better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your asthma was a little flared—we gave you a steroid burst and nebs. Keep using your inhalers at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t used them regularly. I only take them when I wheeze.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s not enough. The Flovent is preventive. You need to use it every day, even when you feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. But honestly, I forget sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go over all your meds before you leave. And social work can help with resources for alcohol support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want to go to rehab. But I’ll try outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good start. Stopping alcohol is the most important thing for your liver and overall health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are better. Potassium is 3.8, phosphate is up. You’re ready to go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds am I taking now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before, plus ferrous sulfate for iron, potassium pill, and the diuretics—furosemide and spironolactone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Suboxone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 1.5 tablets daily. We’re giving you a letter so you can get your next dose without delay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I don’t want to mess that up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Follow up with your PCP in a week for labs and your heart. Hepatology is scheduled for your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no drinking, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s the best thing you can do for your health. We’re here to help—don’t hesitate to reach out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. We’ll send all instructions and prescriptions with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I’ll try to stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We believe in you. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One thing—my skin looks yellow. Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s jaundice, from your liver disease. It’s stable now, but another reason to avoid alcohol completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s all we ask. Take the discharge papers to your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. See you around, I hope not!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ha! Hopefully not. But we’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. And remember—no alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No alcohol. Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're in the hospital because you were having symptoms of alcohol withdrawal. Do you remember coming in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I was shaking bad, and my vision was blurry. I hadn’t had a drink in a few days after drinking a lot. I didn’t think it’d hit me this hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. You’ve had withdrawal issues before, and we take that seriously. We’re starting you on a medication called phenobarbital to help prevent seizures and ease the withdrawal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been sober before—three months clean. I don’t know why I started again. I just… did.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Relapses happen, especially with alcohol use disorder. The important thing is you’re here now, and we’re going to help you get through this safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ve been seeing double sometimes, and little black dots in my vision. Is that from the drinking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking into that. It could be related to withdrawal or your liver. We’ve given you thiamine to prevent complications. Your vision issues seem to be improving, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My liver’s not great, yeah. I’ve got cirrhosis. But I haven’t had bleeding or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right. You did vomit some blood when you came in, but no further episodes. We’re watching that. Your CT scan shows your liver is cirrhotic and you have portal hypertension, but no active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Portal hypertension? What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means there’s increased pressure in the vein that goes to your liver. It can lead to complications like enlarged veins, but we’re monitoring you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve also been short of breath. Is that my asthma?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. Your oxygen levels are lower than normal, especially when you walk. We did a CT and an echo, and it looks like you have something called hepatopulmonary syndrome—your liver disease is affecting your lungs’ ability to oxygenate your blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds serious. Do I need oxygen at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right now, your oxygen is okay with activity. We’ll check again before discharge. If it stays stable, you won’t need home oxygen, but you’ll need follow-up with liver specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your electrolytes are stable. We’re keeping an eye on them because of your history of refeeding syndrome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s refeeding syndrome again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: When someone who’s malnourished starts eating again, their body shifts electrolytes rapidly. It can cause heart or nerve problems. We’re giving you vitamins and monitoring closely to prevent that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been eating much lately. I’ll try to eat more now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll help with that. Nutrition is important, especially with your liver condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound of your liver. It confirms cirrhosis and shows your spleen is enlarged, which is common with portal hypertension.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a sign of advanced liver disease, but we’re managing it. You also have gallstones, but they’re not causing problems now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, more issues. What about my blood counts? They’ve always been low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have pancytopenia—low red cells, white cells, and platelets. It’s likely due to your spleen trapping them and your alcohol use. No transfusions needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your mental status has been a bit off—you were confused about the date when you came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt foggy. I still do a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s called hepatic encephalopathy—your liver isn’t clearing toxins well. We’ve started lactulose and rifaximin to help. It should improve your thinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lactulose gives me diarrhea. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s the goal. It helps remove ammonia from your body. We’ll adjust the dose so you have 2–3 bowel movements a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I guess that’s better than being confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT angiogram to check your lungs and heart. No blood clots, which is good. But it confirms hepatopulmonary syndrome. Also, you have a small aneurysm in a splenic artery—2.1 cm. It’s stable, but we’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An aneurysm? That sounds scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s small and stable. Most don’t rupture. But your liver team will keep an eye on it during your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back clean—no infection. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling better. The shaking’s gone, and my head’s clearer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your phenobarbital taper is almost done. We’re also restarting your buprenorphine for opioid use disorder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on it for years. I didn’t want to stop, but I wasn’t stable when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held it briefly for safety, but now that you’re stable, we’re resuming it. You’ll get eight doses to take home and follow up with your clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re talking about discharge planning. Social work is helping set up a dual diagnosis day program for substance use and mental health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not sure about inpatient, but a day program might work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good step. They can support your sobriety and anxiety. We also discussed acamprosate—it might help reduce cravings, but we’ll decide that outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d like to try. I don’t want to go through this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oxygen levels during walking are better—93% now. So we won’t send you home with oxygen, but keep using your inhalers for asthma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using the nebs when I wheeze. My chest feels better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep your fluticasone and albuterol. Also, your heart function is okay—still diastolic heart failure, so keep taking your diuretics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot them when I was drinking. I’ll take them now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve removed potassium from your meds since your levels are normal. But keep taking your vitamins, iron, and thiamine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow you’ll be discharged. We’ll give you naloxone in case of opioid overdose—important for safety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know how to use it. I’ve had it before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Also, you got hepatitis A and B vaccines while here. You’ll need follow-up doses in one and six months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know I needed those.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: With cirrhosis, they’re important to prevent further liver damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What else do I need to do after I leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take all your meds, especially lactulose and rifaximin. Follow up with hepatology, your PCP, and the day program. And please—no alcohol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I don’t want to end up back here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you. You’ve made progress—clearer mind, stable vitals, and no withdrawal symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you soon. Keep your appointments, take your meds, and reach out if you’re struggling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll try my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You're here because of trouble breathing and chest tightness. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m struggling to catch my breath. It’s been getting worse over the last few days. My chest feels tight, and I’ve had this cough with a runny nose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also mentioned some abdominal and back pain. Any fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. Just the pain and this anxiety that’s been building up. I’ve had asthma attacks before—this feels similar, but worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your breathing is labored, and we hear wheezing all over. Your oxygen level is low, so you’re on 6 liters of oxygen. We did a chest X-ray—it didn’t show pneumonia or fluid, but we’re admitting you to the ICU for close monitoring because of your history of intubations.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been intubated seven times… I don’t want that again. Is it really that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re doing everything to avoid that. You’re getting continuous albuterol, magnesium, and high-dose steroids through an IV. These help open your airways and reduce inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… and my liver issues? I know my cirrhosis can complicate things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware of your cirrhosis and hepatopulmonary syndrome. Your platelets are low, and your liver enzymes are elevated, but stable. We’re being cautious with medications and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We moved you to the regular floor—you’re doing better. Your breathing is still labored, but you don’t need ICU-level care anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I still feel puffed out. Did the tests show what’s going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan showed new ground-glass opacities in both lungs—most prominent in the right upper lobe. It’s not typical of just asthma. We’re concerned about pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pneumonia? But I don’t have a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not all pneumonia causes fever, especially with your immune status. We started broad antibiotics just in case. We also did a sputum test—we’ll know more in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sputum culture came back: it’s Haemophilus influenzae, a common bacteria. It’s sensitive to ampicillin, so we’re switching your antibiotic to ceftriaxone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s bacterial, not viral? Does that mean I’m contagious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s bacterial, but not highly contagious. You’re on treatment now, so risk is low. We’ll keep you isolated until we’re sure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve also noticed my legs are swelling more. And I’ve been waking up gasping—like I can’t breathe lying down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ve developed fluid overload—likely from the high-dose steroids. We’re starting IV furosemide to help you pee out the extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Steroids are causing this? But they’re helping my breathing, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. They’re helping your lungs, but they make your body retain fluid. We’re balancing that with diuretics. Your heart function is actually good—EF over 75%—so it’s not heart failure causing this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adjusting your diuretics. Your spironolactone dose was increased to help with fluid, but your potassium went up. We’re lowering it back to your home dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My potassium’s high? I thought I always needed supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Spironolactone can raise potassium, especially with cirrhosis. We’ll monitor it closely. Your sodium also dropped—we think due to fluid overload. Diuresis should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is improving. The pulmonology team recommends switching from IV steroids to oral prednisone. You’ll be on a taper—start high, then slowly decrease over weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be on it? Last time I was on steroids, I had terrible anxiety and couldn’t sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. That’s why we’re starting sertraline, an SSRI for anxiety. It takes a few weeks to work, but it’s safer long-term than benzodiazepines. We’ll keep lorazepam available for breakthrough anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I’ve been trying to stay off alcohol—last drink was about three weeks ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’re continuing your thiamine, folic acid, and multivitamins. We’ll talk about acamprosate later—helps with alcohol cravings, safer than naltrexone in cirrhosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows improvement in the right upper lobe opacity. The antibiotics are working. Your oxygen needs are down—you’re on room air now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to make sure your fluid levels are stable, finish your antibiotic course, and get your prednisone taper planned. Also, your Suboxone—we need to confirm the dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was taking it once a day, but I think I should be on twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we spoke with your PCP. You’ll go home on twice daily. We’ll also start you on new inhalers—Symbicort and Spiriva—to better control your asthma long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your sodium is improving, and potassium is back to normal. We’re switching your furosemide and spironolactone to once daily for now, to avoid further electrolyte issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to stay on once daily forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. We’ll recheck your labs in a week. If they’re stable, your PCP may restart twice daily dosing if needed for fluid control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. You’re off IV meds, breathing comfortably, and your weight is down—good sign the fluid is resolving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Still some back and shoulder pain, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s your usual chronic pain, aggravated by coughing and labored breathing. We’ve continued your gabapentin and methocarbamol. Avoid extra opioids now that you’re on Suboxone twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we noticed white patches in your mouth this morning. It looks like thrush, a type of yeast infection. Common with steroids and cirrhosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s sore. What will you give me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Clotrimazole troches—dissolve in your mouth four times a day. Should clear it up in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows continued improvement. The pulmonologist reviewed your case—we’ll discharge you tomorrow if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great news. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish your prednisone taper—30 mg for four days, then 20, 10, 5, then stop. Take your new inhalers daily. Monitor your weight and watch for swelling or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your PCP in one week for labs—sodium, potassium, liver tests. Also schedule with pulmonology and hepatology. We’ll send referrals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update: your labs are stable, breathing is good, and you’re eating well. We’re clearing you for discharge today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—here’s your discharge summary. You’re on prednisone taper, sertraline, Suboxone twice daily, and new inhalers. Take all meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll call if I have trouble breathing or swelling comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And if mouth sores worsen, or you feel confused—could be liver or electrolyte issues. Otherwise, we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay well, and keep up the good work with your recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check—how’s your breathing now compared to when you came in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I can take deep breaths without wheezing. Still a little tired, but I’ll rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Healing takes time. Keep using your inhalers, and don’t skip doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful. And no alcohol—I know it makes everything worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best thing you can do. Your liver and lungs will thank you. We’re proud of your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate that. I’m motivated to stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That attitude will take you far. We’ll be in touch with your PCP to coordinate care. Take care, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Looking forward to it. Take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Bye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. Rest well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. Stay healthy.
